target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for working Americans.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers, especially low-income workers in retail, food service, gig, or other essential jobs, paid or even protected time off; many would still have to work or lose wages to vote, so the holiday may do little for the people who most need it.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would significantly increase turnout and function as an effective access reform.
objection: Election Day being a holiday, by itself, is not a reliable turnout strategy; research and practical logic suggest reforms that directly address voting barriers, such as protected time off to vote and automatic voter registration, are more dependable.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a national holiday is the right solution instead of other reforms.
objection: State laws requiring employer time off to vote, protected time during the workday, and automatic voter registration would be more direct and dependable ways to increase access than simply declaring a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday is ineffective because it does not guarantee paid leave in the private sector.
objection: Even if a holiday does not guarantee paid leave, it still increases the availability of time to vote by making schools, routine services, and many workplaces more likely to close or shift to holiday schedules, which reduces scheduling conflicts.

target: AG2’s assumption that caregiving and school routines are irrelevant to the holiday question.
objection: A holiday also helps parents and guardians because school schedules and other caregiving-related routines often change, making it easier to coordinate child care and get to the polls.

target: AG2’s framing of the choice as holiday versus better reforms.
objection: That is a false choice: Election Day can be made a national holiday and still be paired with stronger voting-access reforms such as workplace time-off protections and automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday increases the availability of time and can be paired with other reforms.
objection: A federal holiday still does not reliably convert into paid or protected time for low-income workers, because many essential or service-sector workplaces remain open and workers on shifts, rotating schedules, or gig work can still face the same vote-versus-wages conflict.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling barriers for everyone.
objection: A holiday only helps when employers actually close; many low-income workers in retail, food service, caregiving, transportation, and other essential jobs still have to work, so the holiday mainly changes the calendar without solving the underlying constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday addresses the main voting barrier.
objection: Voting access is broader than having a day off; a holiday does not fix registration friction, poll confusion, transportation and accessibility problems, or long lines, so it is unlikely to be the most impactful reform.

target: AG2’s claim that because the holiday may not be paid or universally observed, it is not worthwhile.
objection: Lack of paid leave does not mean no benefit: even unpaid, a holiday reduces the need to fit voting into narrow windows and gives people more flexibility around work, childcare, and other routines.

target: AG2’s assumption that essential workplaces staying open makes the holiday insignificant.
objection: Although some essential workplaces remain open, holiday scheduling still changes opening hours and coverage in many places, so the policy would still meaningfully reduce conflicts for many workers even if not everyone benefits equally.

target: AG2’s presentation of holiday versus workplace reforms as mutually exclusive.
objection: This is a false choice because a national holiday can be combined with the state or federal workplace voting-time protections AG2 wants; the holiday can be a baseline reform rather than a substitute for others.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday’s main value is reduced scheduling pressure.
objection: If a holiday still does not guarantee paid or protected time, then the decisive reform is the enforceable time-off policy, not the holiday label itself; without that, the holiday risks being only an add-on or distraction.

target: AG2’s claim that only protected time off matters and a holiday is unnecessary.
objection: A national holiday is a nationwide scheduling reset that reduces individual negotiation and improvisation, making it easier for people to coordinate voting even when time off is unpaid or workplaces are partly open.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is valuable even without guaranteed paid leave.
objection: A holiday without enforceable job-protected time does not reliably help low-income workers; employers still control schedules, and workers may still be forced to choose between wages and voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday materially lowers bottlenecks and peak congestion.
objection: A holiday does not directly fix polling-place capacity, staffing, transportation, or accessibility barriers, so it may shift when people vote without addressing the true access bottlenecks.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday cannot improve the election system itself.
objection: A national holiday can help poll workers, election offices, schools, and civic organizations plan and staff the day more effectively, which can reduce lines and wait times in addition to easing voters’ schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that smoother election-day administration makes the holiday a high-value reform.
objection: Even if election administration is smoother, the holiday still does not reliably give low-income private-sector workers enforceable time to vote, so smoother operations do not solve the main wage-and-schedule barrier.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday meaningfully boosts turnout or access on its own.
objection: Improving polling-place operations does not ensure turnout if workers cannot leave their jobs or cannot afford lost wages; the holiday may reduce lines but still leave the core access problem intact.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday should be a broad baseline reform.
objection: Treating the holiday as a first-step baseline may waste political capital and attention that could go directly to more reliable measures, especially if evidence suggests an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy.
